---
title: "Centaur or cyborg: what you hand to the machine, and what you keep"
subtitle: "AIM-5 · AIM-X · AIM-4 · about 90 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. Sort the tasks on an intern's list into three kinds of use, with a
   justification for each that names the task's risk and whether any tool has
   been validated for it.
2. Tell deskilling from never-skilling from mis-skilling, and name one task in
   your own coming internship at risk from each.
3. Rewrite an answer-seeking prompt as a hint-seeking one using the Who / Where
   / What scaffold, and say what the rewrite made you do that the original did
   not.
4. State what the randomized trials of physicians working with a language model
   found, what the randomized studies of learners found, and name two techniques
   that counter the second finding.
5. Say what you document, and to whom you disclose, when a machine drafted
   something that carries your signature.
6. Write down which part of clinical judgment you will not delegate, and why.
:::

**Time.** About 30 minutes of reading, 25 minutes of listening, 30 minutes of
doing, and five minutes at the end that you should not skip. You need one
general-purpose chatbot for the second half of the Do; your institutional
ChatGPT Edu or Microsoft Copilot account is enough. The first half of the Do
needs only a pen. Nothing installs.

## The first list

It is 6:10 on the first Monday of intern year. You have six patients, a
badge that opens more doors than it should, and a list.

```{=html}
<div style="max-width:520px;margin:1.2em auto;padding:1em 1.3em;background:#fffdf5;border:1px solid #e0d9c3;border-left:6px solid #c9a227;font-family:'Segoe UI',Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;box-shadow:2px 2px 0 #e0d9c3;">
<div style="font-size:.75em;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:#7a6a3a;">Mon · day 1 · before rounds</div>
<ol style="margin:.5em 0 .3em 1.2em;padding:0;line-height:1.55;">
<li>Pre-round: beds 4, 7, 9, 12, 14, 15. Overnight events, vitals, labs.</li>
<li>Progress notes x6 before 8:00.</li>
<li>Discharge summary, bed 12 (admitted 11 days ago; three services involved).</li>
<li>Portal inbox: four patient messages from the weekend.</li>
<li>Call nephrology about bed 9 &mdash; what exactly are we asking?</li>
<li>Journal club slides, Thursday. Have not picked the paper.</li>
</ol>
<div style="font-size:.7em;color:#8a7a5a;border-top:1px solid #e0d9c3;padding-top:.4em;margin-top:.4em;">Illustrative intern task list for this chapter. No patient on it is real.</div>
</div>
```

Your senior resident, who has been an intern for exactly one year, looks at the
list and says the thing every senior says now: "Have it draft the notes. Have it
draft the discharge summary. That's what it's for." She means the assistant
built into the chart, the one with the sparkle icon, or the institutional
chatbot in the other tab. She is not wrong that it can. Last week, on your
sub-internship, you watched an attending send an AI-drafted reply to a patient
message without reading it. Nobody said whether that was fine.

Look at the list again with one question: for each line, if you hand it to the
machine, what do you get back, and what do you lose? The notes are the easy
case, and even there the answer splits in two, because a note that is *drafted*
for you and a note that is *written* by you are different things wearing the
same template. The discharge summary is the hard case. It is the only document
on the list that forces you to read eleven days of chart and decide what
happened to this person, and that reading is most of what you will know about
them when their primary care doctor calls you next month. The consult question
is a different kind of hard: the machine will produce a very good question, and
the reason you are calling is that you do not yet know what to ask.

This chapter is about that sorting. It does not ask whether you should use
these tools at all; you will meet them in the chart regardless, and "never"
is one of the verdicts available to you for any single line. It asks *what
kind* of use, for *which* task, at *what* risk, and it asks you to write your
answer down.

## Why this matters

In three months, the list above is yours, and the tool will be in the chart
whether or not you have decided how to use it. Health systems are integrating
these assistants into systems you do not control, and you will use them with
increasing regularity, less supervision, and more autonomy, in roughly that
order. Two of this course's faculty, quoted from its prior session, frame the
two ends of it. One put the alternative bluntly at a national
medical-education meeting: you *can* choose to avoid AI, but is that really an
option? (Chad Stickrath, MD). The other, a pediatric hospitalist, said the thing
that keeps this chapter honest: we should be scared, because what we do is
scary (Christina Olson, MD). Both are right.

There is a second reason, and it is specific to where you are standing. You are
about to learn clinical reasoning for the first time, on real patients, with a
tool available that will produce a plausible answer to every question you were
supposed to struggle with. Someone who has practiced for fifteen years and
starts using these tools risks losing a skill. You risk never acquiring it, or
acquiring it wrong. Those are three different problems, and the chapter's most
useful idea is that they need three different defenses.

## The idea

### Two ways to work with a machine

The appraisal chapter left you with a randomized trial and a puzzle. Fifty
physicians were given six diagnostic cases; half also had a language model,
the kind of AI behind ChatGPT and Copilot, which produces text in reply to
text. The physicians with the model did no better than the physicians without it, an
adjusted difference of 2 points on a 100-point reasoning score (95% CI −4 to
8). The model working alone scored 16 points above the physicians (95% CI 2 to
30) [@pmid:39466245].

::: {#fig-goh}

Median diagnostic-reasoning score per case, as a percentage of the rubric, in
the 2024 randomized trial. The model-alone bar is drawn at 74 + 16; the paper
reports the difference, not a median. Redrawn from the published numbers
[@pmid:39466245]; data are not copyrightable.
:::

The tool was capable. The people holding it did not get the benefit. The
authors' own reading is that the gap is a training problem: the "need for
technology and workforce development to realize the potential of
physician–artificial intelligence collaboration." Workforce development means
you.

The same group ran a second trial a year later, on management rather than
diagnosis: 92 physicians, five cases, treatment and testing decisions revealed
in sequence. This time the physicians with the model scored 6.5 points higher
than those without (95% CI 2.7 to 10.2), spent about two minutes longer per
case, and were indistinguishable from the model alone [@pmid:39910272]. Two
trials, same team, same tool class, opposite headline. The variable that
changed was not the model. It was the task, and how the physicians worked
with it.

There is a vocabulary for that variable. It comes from a 2023 field experiment
in which several hundred management consultants were given GPT-4 and the
researchers watched how the successful ones worked [@doi:10.2139/ssrn.4573321].
Two patterns emerged, and the names have stuck:

- A **centaur** divides the work. Like the creature, there is a clean line
  between the human half and the horse half. You assign a bounded piece of the
  task to the machine, keep the rest, and evaluate what comes back before it
  touches anything.
- A **cyborg** blends the work. You move back and forth with the machine inside
  a single piece of work, drafting a sentence, asking for three alternatives,
  taking one, rewriting it, asking what is missing.

Neither is the correct mode. The chess players who first used the word
centaur, after Kasparov's human-plus-computer exhibition matches in the late
1990s, found the same thing within a few years: amateurs with a good process
beat grandmasters with a worse one [VERIFY: Kasparov's own account of the 2005
freestyle tournament; not a peer-reviewed source]{.verify}. The skill is knowing which mode a task calls for, and shifting. The 2025
*NEJM* review this chapter is built on gives the rule of thumb
[@pmid:40834302]: centaur strategies for high-stakes tasks and for tools that
have not been validated for the use you are putting them to; cyborg strategies
where the task is low-risk, creative, or the tool is well validated for exactly
this. @fig-modes is that rule as a decision.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-modes
%%| fig-cap: "Which mode a task calls for. Two questions, asked before you open the tool. Adapted from the framework in Abdulnour et al. (2025)."
flowchart TD
  T["The task in front of you"] --> R{"If the output is wrong,<br/>who is harmed, and how badly?"}
  R -- "A patient, seriously" --> V1{"Is any tool validated<br/>for this exact use,<br/>at your institution?"}
  R -- "Mostly me, or nobody" --> V2{"Is the tool validated<br/>for this use?"}
  V1 -- No --> C1["Centaur, or not at all.<br/>Bounded delegation.<br/>Verify every line."]
  V1 -- Yes --> C2["Centaur.<br/>Delegate the bounded piece.<br/>Verify before signing."]
  V2 -- No --> C3["Cyborg is reasonable.<br/>Stay in the loop.<br/>Check what matters."]
  V2 -- Yes --> C4["Cyborg.<br/>Iterate freely."]
```

"Validated for this use" is a phrase the appraisal chapter spent two hours on.
Here it means one thing: someone has measured how the tool performs on *this*
task, on patients like yours, and you know the number. An ambient scribe,
the tool that listens to a visit and drafts the note, with three randomized
trials behind it is validated for drafting a visit note. The same product is
not validated for writing your discharge summary, and the chatbot in the other
tab is validated for nothing on your list. The validation column will look
different in twelve months; the sorting will not.

### Three ways to lose a skill

The 2025 review names three perils, and they are worth learning as three words
because the defenses differ [@pmid:40834302]:

- **Deskilling**: losing a reasoning skill you had.
- **Never-skilling**: never learning a skill at all, because the tool arrived
  before the skill did.
- **Mis-skilling**: learning an incorrect pattern, because the tool's plausible
  wrong answers became your template.

None of these is hypothetical, and two of them have been measured.

**Deskilling has a number.** At four endoscopy centres in Poland, computer-aided
polyp detection was switched on at the end of 2021. In the three months
*before*, endoscopists doing ordinary colonoscopy without the tool found
adenomas in 28.4% of patients. In the three months *after*, doing the same
colonoscopy on days the tool was off, they found them in 22.4%. That is an
absolute drop of 6 points (95% CI −10.5 to −1.6) in a skill these were experts
at, after a few months of having a machine draw the boxes for them
[@pmid:40816301]. The study is observational and the authors say "might," but
the direction is the one every clinician who has stopped reading their own ECGs
would predict.

**Never-skilling has a trial.** Nearly a thousand high-school students in
Turkey were randomized, during maths practice sessions, to no AI, a plain
GPT-4 chat, or a GPT-4 "tutor" prompted to give hints rather than answers.
While they had the tool, both AI groups did far better on practice problems:
48% higher scores with the plain chat, 127% with the tutor. Then the tool was
taken away for the exam. The plain-chat students scored 17% *worse* than the
students who had never had access. The tutor group's losses were largely
eliminated [@pmid:40560616]. The authors' word for what the plain chat became
is *crutch*. The finding is not that the tool did not work. The thing it
improved and the thing the students needed were not the same thing.

**Mis-skilling has no trial yet**, which is why the chapter draws it instead.
Below is a progress note drafted by an assistant from a fictional chart. The
patient is invented; the note is the kind you will be handed. Read the plan.

```{=html}
<div style="max-width:600px;margin:1.2em auto;padding:0;border:1px solid #cfd6df;border-radius:6px;font-family:Menlo,Consolas,'Courier New',monospace;font-size:.82em;background:#f8fafc;box-shadow:0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,.12);">
<div style="background:#1565c0;color:#fff;padding:.45em .9em;font-family:'Segoe UI',Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;font-size:.9em;display:flex;justify-content:space-between;"><span>&#10024; Draft progress note &middot; hospital day 3</span><span style="opacity:.8">Accept &middot; Edit &middot; Discard</span></div>
<div style="padding:.8em 1em;line-height:1.5;color:#222;white-space:pre-wrap;">S: Pt reports breathing "a little better." Slept flat x2 pillows. No CP.
O: T 37.1 HR 88 BP 118/70 RR 18 SpO2 94% RA. Wt 84.2 kg (admit 87.0).
   JVP 8 cm. Bibasilar crackles, improved. 1+ pedal edema.
   Na 133 K 3.4 Cr 1.6 (baseline 1.0; yesterday 1.3) BUN 41.
   BNP trending down. CXR: improving vascular congestion.
A/P:
1. Acute decompensated HFrEF, improving. Continue furosemide 80 mg IV BID.
   Daily weights, strict I/O. Goal net negative 1-1.5 L.
<span style="background:#fff4cc;display:block;margin:0 -1em;padding:0 1em;">2. AKI, likely prerenal in setting of poor PO intake and diuresis.
   Continue IV fluids at 75 mL/h. Trend Cr. Hold nephrotoxins.</span>
3. Hypokalemia. Replete K to &gt;4.0.
4. HTN. Continue home lisinopril.
Dispo: continue inpatient diuresis.</div>
<div style="padding:.4em 1em;border-top:1px solid #cfd6df;font-family:'Segoe UI',Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;font-size:.85em;color:#5a6a7a;">Illustrative draft for this chapter, written for a fictional patient. Not the output of any real product.</div>
</div>
```

Problem 2 is fluent, correctly formatted, and internally contradictory with
problem 1: the plan diurets the patient and hydrates them in the same note.
The rise in creatinine on day 3 of diuresis is the expected cost of getting
fluid off a congested kidney, and the decision an intern is supposed to make
here, and to be quizzed on at rounds, is whether to hold the diuretic, slow it,
or push through. The draft made a decision by template. If you accept it, you
have a note with a wrong plan. If you accept it on ten patients, you have a
pattern: creatinine up, add fluids. That is mis-skilling, and the tell is that
nothing about the sentence looks wrong. It looks like every other note.

| Peril | What it is | The intern task most exposed | The defense |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Deskilling** | A skill you had erodes with disuse | Reading your own images, ECGs, and strips before the machine's read | Do it first, then look. Keep a count of where you disagreed and who was right. |
| **Never-skilling** | A skill you never build because the tool answered first | The differential; the consult question; the discharge summary's narrative | Start on your own. Ask for hints. Take the tool away before the test, because residency will. |
| **Mis-skilling** | A wrong pattern learned from plausible output | Any drafted assessment and plan | Read the reasoning, not the conclusion. Ask *why this and not that*. Never accept a plan you could not have written. |

: Three perils, three defenses. The middle row is where a fourth-year is most exposed. {#tbl-perils}

### The learners' study, and six techniques

The Turkish trial measured grades. A separate randomized study measured what
learners *do*. It compared students working with a chatbot, with a human
expert, and with a checklist tool, and recorded their behaviour as well as
their scores. The chatbot group performed better on the immediate task and did
not gain more knowledge, motivation, or ability to transfer what they learned.
The authors' name for the behaviour that explained the gap is *metacognitive
laziness*: offloading the monitoring and evaluation of one's own thinking to
the tool [@doi:10.1111/bjet.13544]. Metacognition is the ordinary word for
noticing what you know and do not know; laziness is not a moral judgment, it
is what any of us does when a faster path exists.

The same authors' answer to "should learners use these tools?" is *probably,
yes*. The course's prior session turned their recommendations into five
techniques, and added a sixth. They are the defense against never-skilling in
@tbl-perils, made specific:

1. **Start on your own.** Build your differential before you ask anything.
   The grappling is the part that does the learning. Consult when genuinely
   stuck, not when merely uncertain.
2. **Ask for hints, not answers.** Not "give me the differential for this
   presentation," but "I have anchored on a cardiac cause and I think I am
   missing something in the abdomen; what categories should I be considering
   that I have not named?"
3. **Teach back.** State your reasoning in your own words and ask whether it
   is right, rather than asking for the reasoning to be supplied.
4. **Focus on the why.** Why this agent and not that one, why this cutoff,
   why first-line. The reason is what makes the knowledge portable to the next
   patient.
5. **Use the four patterns deliberately.** Explanation of something you
   already read; debugging your own reasoning after it failed; conceptual
   clarification; and learning a better approach *after* you have solved the
   problem yourself.
6. **Ask it to quiz you.** The mode in which the tool tests you is the one
   least able to produce dependence, and it inverts the relationship in the
   opening quote of the prior session, where a student described comparing
   their own thinking against the machine's "as if the program is a mentor or
   learner."

### Who, where, what

Half of the difference between a hint and an answer is in the prompt, and if
English is not your first language or you are new to these tools, the
difference is not obvious. The scaffold the course uses has three parts:

- **Who** you are: "I am a fourth-year medical student."
- **Where** you are: "I am on an inpatient medicine rotation, day 3 of a
  patient admitted with a heart-failure exacerbation."
- **What** you want, phrased as the thing you want to *understand* rather than
  the thing you want *produced*: "I want to understand how to think about a
  rising creatinine during diuresis, and I want you to ask me what I think
  first."

Here is the same request both ways, for the fictional patient above.

::: {.callout-note title="Answer-seeking"}
> 67M with HFrEF exacerbation, day 3 of IV furosemide, creatinine 1.0 → 1.3 →
> 1.6. What should I do about the AKI?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint-seeking"}
> I am a fourth-year medical student on an inpatient medicine rotation. My
> patient was admitted three days ago with a heart-failure exacerbation and is
> being diuresed; weight is down 3 kg, still has crackles and edema, and
> creatinine has gone from 1.0 to 1.6. I think this is expected cardiorenal
> physiology and I want to keep diuresing, but I am not confident. Do not tell
> me what to do. Ask me two questions that would change your mind, then tell me
> what I have missed.
:::

The first prompt gets a plan, and the plan will sometimes be the one in the
draft note. The second gets a conversation in which you have to say what you
think before the tool says anything, which is the only arrangement in which
being wrong teaches you something.

### The practical rules, in the order you will need them

This section is for the reader who skipped the mechanism. Each rule has a
reason and a boundary.

**You sign the note.** Whatever drafted it, the signature is yours, and so is
the accountability. In every chart-review, malpractice, and quality-committee
process that exists today, the question is what the signing clinician knew and
did, not what the software suggested. The boundary: a tool your institution
licenses and runs inside the EHR, the electronic health record, is covered by a business associate agreement,
the contract that makes a vendor legally responsible for protecting patient
data, and is governed by an institutional policy that may say how to document
its use. Ask what that policy says in your first week. The chatbot in the other
tab has no such agreement, and your institutional login does not change that
unless your institution says it does.

**No patient information in a consumer tool, ever.** Not a name, not a
paraphrase of a case with the name removed, not a screenshot. The temptation
you will feel is time pressure at 6:10 a.m. The rule holds. A fictional case
constructed to make the same teaching point is always available, and this
chapter gives you one.

**Document what you did, in the language your institution uses.** Some systems
add a line to AI-drafted notes and messages automatically; some require the
clinician to attest; some say nothing yet. [VERIFY: current attestation and
disclosure language at the course institution; policies differ by system and
change yearly]{.verify} The durable rule is that you should be able to answer
"did a tool draft this?" honestly and without hesitation, to a patient, an
attending, or a lawyer, and that the answer should already be in the record if
your institution has a place for it.

**Disclosure to the patient is a separate question from documentation.** The
attending who sent the unread draft made two decisions: not to read it, and not
to tell the patient. The second is the one the patient would care about, and it
is the subject of the patient-communication chapter. Here, one number: when a
large academic system turned on AI-drafted replies for 162 clinicians, the
drafts were used for about 20% of replies, reply time did not change, and
clinicians' task load and exhaustion fell significantly [@pmid:38506805]. The
tool reduced burden without saving time, which is what you would expect if the
clinicians were reading and editing the drafts. That is the centaur version of the task. Sending unread is
not a mode; it is an absence of one.

**The one sentence for a co-intern.** *If you could not have written it, do not
sign it.* That sentence covers the drafted note, the discharge summary, the
consult question, and the portal reply, and it is the operational form of the
third row in @tbl-perils.

### Shared inquiry, not authority

One more thing from the *NEJM* review, and it changes how you should read your
own supervisors in three months. The authors note that supervisors often have
less expertise with these tools than their learners, and recommend shared
inquiry rather than performed authority [@pmid:40834302]. The structure they
propose for the conversation is a debrief you will be on the receiving end of,
so learn it now.

::: {.callout-note title="DEFT-AI: the debrief"}
- **D**iagnosis, or discussion: what was your reasoning, and how did the tool
  assist?
- **E**vidence: how did you verify?
- **F**eedback: what could improve?
- **T**eaching: what did you learn, about the tool and about reasoning?
- **AI** recommendation: what are the next steps for safe use?

Five questions; the second is the one that matters. If the honest answer to
"how did you verify?" is "I did not," the rest of the debrief writes itself.
:::

The review names one more thing the perils above depend on, and calls it the
foundation: **adaptive expertise**, the capacity to shift between efficient
routine practice and slower, innovative problem-solving. Critical thinking, in
their account, has to be taught, modeled, and assessed *during* AI use rather
than assumed to survive it. That is the reason this course exists and the
reason this chapter ends with you writing a policy rather than reading one.

## Watch or listen

**Podcast.** *NEJM AI Grand Rounds*, episode 35, "Medicine, Machines, and Magic:
Dr. Jonathan Chen on Medical AI" (October 15, 2025; 48 min).
<https://ai-podcast.nejm.org/e/medicine-machines-and-magic-dr-jonathan-chen-on-medical-ai/>

Chen is the senior author of both randomized trials above. Budget 25 minutes.
Listen for three things: his own account of why the model beat the physicians
in the first trial and why the second trial came out differently; what he says
about automation anxiety, which is the emotional register of the perils
section; and the claim, in the episode's own summary, that empathy rather than
memorization may become the most valuable clinical skill. Then ask the question
this chapter asks: which of the tasks on the list at 6:10 a.m. does that claim
actually change, and which does it leave exactly where it was?

**Alternative.** *NEJM AI Grand Rounds*, "AI and the Evolution of Medical
Thought with Dr. Adam Rodman" (June 19, 2024).
<https://ai-podcast.nejm.org/e/ai-and-the-evolution-of-medical-thought-with-dr-adam-rodman>
Rodman is a co-author on both trials and a historian of clinical reasoning; the
episode is the longer view of what clinicians have delegated to instruments
before, and what happened to the skill each time.
[VERIFY: episode length before assigning]{.verify}

## Do

::: {.callout-warning title="No patient information, ever"}
Part A needs no tool. Part B uses the fictional patient from this chapter, or
a fictional case you write yourself. Do not use a patient from your
sub-internship, a classmate's case, or a de-identified real chart. Consumer
and institutional chatbots alike are outside the business associate agreement
that covers the EHR, and free tiers may use what you type to train the next
model.
:::

### Part A: your policy (20 minutes)

This is the chapter's artifact, and it is a set of positions, not evaluations.
You will be asked to reread it in the final session of the course.

**Step 1. Sort the eight tasks.** These are the tasks from the course's prior
session, and they are the list at 6:10 a.m. with the phone call and the
pre-rounding folded in. For each one, write a verdict, a risk, whether you
know of a validated tool for it, the peril it exposes you to most, and one
sentence of justification. Copy the grid into a document.

```
Task                              Mode (centaur / cyborg / not at all)
                                  Risk if wrong (patient / me / nobody)
                                  Validated tool at my institution? (Y / N / don't know)
                                  Peril (deskill / never-skill / mis-skill)
                                  One-sentence rule

1. Drafting a progress note       ______  ______  ______  ______  ______________________
2. Writing a progress note        ______  ______  ______  ______  ______________________
3. Literature search              ______  ______  ______  ______  ______________________
4. Building a differential        ______  ______  ______  ______  ______________________
5. Patient education handout      ______  ______  ______  ______  ______________________
6. Journal club slides            ______  ______  ______  ______  ______________________
7. Summarizing a paper            ______  ______  ______  ______  ______________________
8. Answering a patient message    ______  ______  ______  ______  ______________________

The task on this list I would add: _________________________________
Its row: ______  ______  ______  ______  ______________________
```

The first two rows are deliberately a pair. If you gave them the same verdict,
stop and ask what the difference is between a task where a human is already
holding the pen and one where nobody is. Most of the learning in this exercise
is in that pair.

For row 3, if you want a real search to sort rather than an imagined one, use
this pattern with your specialty as the variable and take the first paper that
fits your journal-club slot:

```
("large language model" OR "artificial intelligence") AND <your specialty>
AND (validation OR "external validation")
```

Filter to the last three years. The paper counts toward this week's resource
log.

**Step 2. Add two columns.** For every row you marked *centaur* or *cyborg*,
write what you would document and to whom you would disclose. "Nothing" and
"nobody" are acceptable answers if you can say why. For row 8, answer for the
patient specifically.

**Step 3. Find your disagreement.** Pick the row you are least sure of. Write
the strongest case for the opposite verdict, in two sentences, as if a
co-intern were making it. Then say whether you have changed your mind, and on
what grounds. An unresolved disagreement written down with both positions is a
better artifact than a forced answer.

### Part B: the prompt (10 minutes)

**Step 1. Take the task you rated most cyborg-appropriate.** Write the prompt
you would actually type, the fast version, the one you would type at 6:10 a.m.
Keep it.

**Step 2. Rewrite it with Who / Where / What**, so that it asks for a hint, a
question, or a check on your reasoning rather than the finished product. Use
the fictional heart-failure patient above if the task needs a case, or write
your own in three lines with no real person in it.

**Step 3. Run the second prompt.** Then, in the same conversation, type: "Now
quiz me on this. Three questions, one at a time, and tell me when I am wrong."
Answer them.

**Step 4. Record it.**

```
Task: ____________________________________________

Fast prompt (as I would have typed it):
______________________________________________________________

Rewritten prompt (Who / Where / What, hint-seeking):
______________________________________________________________
______________________________________________________________

One thing the rewritten prompt made me do that the fast one would not have:
______________________________________________________________

Of the three quiz questions, the one I got wrong, and why:
______________________________________________________________
```

If the tool answered the rewritten prompt with a finished plan anyway, note
that. It happens, and it is the reason "ask for hints" is a technique rather
than a setting.

::: {.callout-tip title="If you have ten minutes and no appetite for the chatbot"}
Do Step 1 of Part A and nothing else. The sort is a judgment task, not a tool
task, and a completed grid with honest "don't know" entries in the validation
column is the whole point. The tool can wait until you have decided what you
would let it do.
:::

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Eight sorted tasks | Each verdict names the risk and the validation status, and the draft/write pair has different verdicts or a stated reason they do not | Verdicts without risk or validation; the pair sorted together without comment |
| A peril per row | Deskilling, never-skilling, and mis-skilling each appear at least once, on a task where that peril fits | One word used for every row |
| Documentation and disclosure columns | Row 8 answers for the patient, and "nothing" is justified where it appears | Columns blank or "N/A" |
| A written disagreement | The opposing case is one a co-intern could actually make, and your verdict states its grounds | A strawman, or "I still think I'm right" |
| Two prompts | The rewrite says who, where, and what, and asks for a hint or a question rather than the product | The rewrite is the fast prompt with "please" added |
| The two findings | You can say what the two physician trials found, what the two learner studies found, and why they are not in conflict | "AI is better than doctors" or "AI hurts learning" alone |
| Two techniques | Two of the six, in your own words, with the peril each defends against | "Be careful" |
| The one sentence | *If you could not have written it, do not sign it*, and you can say which task on the list it bites hardest | Only the slogan |

## The standing question

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Go back to 6:10 a.m. The
senior resident has said "have it draft the notes," and she is waiting. Your
grid is your answer, but say it in two sentences she could repeat: which lines
on the list go to the machine, in which mode, and which one line does not go at
all.

Then the sentence this course collects and rereads in the final session. *Which
part of clinical judgment will you not delegate, and why?* Write it, date it,
and keep a copy where you will find it in four weeks and, ideally, in four
years. Not a category ("patient care") and not a slogan. A task, and a reason.
If you cannot yet name one, write that down instead; it is an honest answer,
and it is the one this chapter most wants you to revisit.

## Summary

- The question is not whether to use the tool but what kind of use, for which
  task, at what risk. Centaur divides and verifies; cyborg blends and
  iterates; the task's risk and the tool's validation decide which.
- In one randomized trial physicians with a model did no better than
  physicians without it while the model alone did; in a second, on management
  tasks, they did better. The model was not the variable. How they worked with
  it was.
- Deskilling, never-skilling, and mis-skilling are three problems with three
  defenses. A fourth-year is most exposed to the middle one.
- Randomized studies of learners find the tool improves the task and not the
  learning; hint-seeking, teach-back, and being quizzed are the techniques that
  close that gap.
- You sign the note. Institutional tools are covered by an agreement and a
  policy; the chatbot in the other tab is covered by neither.
- If you could not have written it, do not sign it.
- The list at 6:10 a.m. is yours in three months. The sort is yours now.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The review this chapter is built on, with the three perils, adaptive
  expertise, and DEFT-AI in full [@pmid:40834302].
- The two physician trials: diagnosis [@pmid:39466245] and management
  [@pmid:39910272]. Read the discussion sections for what the physicians
  actually did with the tool.
- Never-skilling in a randomized field experiment [@pmid:40560616], and
  deskilling in a multicentre observational study [@pmid:40816301].
- The learner study that named metacognitive laziness
  [@doi:10.1111/bjet.13544]; the implications section is written for teachers
  and is the source of the six techniques.
- The consultants' experiment that gave centaur and cyborg their current
  meaning [@doi:10.2139/ssrn.4573321]. Not medicine, and worth reading for the
  finding that the tool helped most on tasks inside its competence and hurt on
  tasks just outside it, which the authors call the jagged frontier.
- AI-drafted patient replies at scale: no time saved, burden reduced, drafts
  read and edited [@pmid:38506805].

**Talks**

- [Prompt engineering](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-17-prompt-engineering/):
  ten rules with clinical examples throughout. Who / Where / What is a
  compression of the first three.
- [AI in medical education](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-23-ai-in-medical-education/):
  attribution and academic integrity, for the moment one of these tools drafts
  something with your name on it outside the hospital.
